CHART OF THE DAY: With a day to go, China's seaborne crude oil imports in September are hovering at just over 7m b/d (down from Aug and Jul, but up from Jun). 

The cumulative drop in Chinese buying (vs 2025 average) has now reached 600 million barrels. Even if seaborne oil imports pick up to 8.5m b/d in 4Q, China would import **nearly 1 billion fewer barrels** than it would have done on last year's pace.

EUROPE’s gasoil prices have climbed to one of the highest levels on record even after adjusting for inflation. Front-month gasoil futures have averaged more than €1270 per tonne so far in September, the third highest on record after October and June 2022, and higher than during the oil price spike in 2008. The continued disruption of crude and fuel exports through the Strait of Hormuz combined with Ukraine’s attacks on Russia’s oil refineries and the relative weakness of the euro against the dollar have all contributed to near-record high prices. Would love to hear from those who believe that the rising Hormuz oil flows **aren't** evidence that Tehran is gradually losing it's capacity to effectively threaten/throttle the Strait.

Why else would Iran "tolerate" those rising flows?

One (largely unprovable) theory I've heard is that Tehran is getting paid off. But that doesn't feel right given that pace of recent gains, the lack of Iranian participation in said trade, etc.

Any other theories?

Note: if you claim that no oil is getting through Hormuz and that all the data is fake news I'm probably not going to weight your views very credibly.

Very thankful and appreciate the many thoughtful, reasoned replies to this question—encourage everyone to read a bunch of them for a wide array of views. 

Lots to chew on, and will be writing up some of the best arguments in our Friday weekly. The most compelling argument to me is (as per @gbrew24) that Tehran is pursuing a very specific and delicate attritional strategy, and (as per @DejikaDonatova) doing so in a cost-optimized manner (ie a handful of drones per week keeping all of CENTCOM preoccupied at great cost to both US taxpayers and commercial shippers).

@yarbatman also made some good points about the Iranian diplomatic/economic relations in the Gulf/China that become more important in a longer-lived conflict in which Tehran failed to get the job done with the initial Hormuz squeeze.

Many also cited Tehran’s lack of appetite to return to a full-blown shooting war, which would risk Iran’s critical infrastructure and predictably spiral into pushing Tehran to hit other upstream Gulf infrastructure that it may regret in the future. And that doing more than it is currently doing in Hormuz risks slipping back into that dangerous tit-for-tat spiral.

The attritional strategy bit seems correct, but it also is inherently an admittance that Iran can no longer so easily control flows through Hormuz;  growing [necessary] risk tolerance from Gulf shippers means that flow effect of a given drone strike is probably only 10-20% of what it would have been a few months ago.

At the end of the day, crude prices remain high (and steeply backwardated/tight) and diesel prices much, much higher—at least for now. Sure, the very high cost of shipping barrels through Hormuz prevents prices from collapsing *too much* before the incentive collapses unless exporters cut price to the bone—but at the end of the day more oil exiting Hormuz, especially the pace continues to steadily rise as it has been, will eventually arrest the current market-pressed urgency.

Imho the test will eventually come in October/November when these rising flows again begin to weigh on prices and structure (as we saw in June/July). Will Tehran be able to reestablish and stick-handle a return of pressure when needed? Or will it have already lost the plot and ceded the necessary fear to get the job done?

Thanks again to everyone who replied and shared thoughts, you folks are all awesome.

Energy delivered another strong month despite the recent retracement, gaining 8.5% and helping offset losses across all other major sectors, most notably precious metals at –6.2% and soft commodities at –8.5%.

At the individual level, Brent and gasoil gained around 12.5%, while the biggest losses were seen in cocoa at –20%, cotton –15%, wheat –10% and silver –8%. Notably, the steep backwardation across energy markets provided a substantial boost to total returns: excluding the positive roll yield, the BCOM Energy Spot Index gained only 4.8%, compared with the 8.3% total-return gain.

Crude oil exports from the Middle East are up, but vehicles run on gasoline and diesel, not crude oil. Crude must first be refined, and refining is a bottleneck right now. The largest tankers departing the region have top priority but they carry crude, not fuel.
